title: Navigating the Grey Area: How Expressions of Uncertainty and Overconfidence Affect Language Models
abstract: The increased deployment of LMs for real-world tasks involving knowledge and facts makes it important to understand model epistemology: what LMs think they know, and how their attitudes toward that knowledge are affected by language use in their inputs. Here, we study an aspect of model epistemology: how epistemic markers of certainty, uncertainty, or evidentiality like "I'm sure it's", "I think it's", or "Wikipedia says it's" affect models, and whether they contribute to model failures. We develop a typology of epistemic markers and inject 50 markers into prompts for question answering. We find that LMs are highly sensitive to epistemic markers in prompts, with accuracies varying more than 80%. Surprisingly, we find that expressions of high certainty result in a 7% decrease in accuracy as compared to low certainty expressions; similarly, factive verbs hurt performance, while evidentials benefit performance. Our analysis of a popular pretraining dataset shows that these markers of uncertainty are associated with answers on question-answering websites, while markers of certainty are associated with questions. These associations may suggest that the behavior of LMs is based on mimicking observed language use, rather than truly reflecting epistemic uncertainty.

claims.text: Language models are highly sensitive to epistemic markers in prompts, with question-answering accuracy varying by up to 80% depending on the marker used.
Expressions of high certainty in prompts lead to lower question-answering accuracy compared to expressions of low certainty.
Factive verbs in prompt templates consistently decrease language model accuracy across question-answering datasets.
Evidential markers in prompt templates significantly improve language model generation accuracy across multiple datasets.
In question-answering pretraining data, expressions of uncertainty occur roughly twice as often in answer posts as in question posts.
In question-answering pretraining data, expressions of certainty occur more than twice as often in question posts as in answer posts.
The perplexity of epistemic prompt templates does not correlate with generated accuracy (Pearson's ρ = -0.03).
Prompting with weakeners leads to higher entropy across candidate non-top predictions compared to prompting with strengtheners.
Numerical uncertainty expressions in prompts show poor linguistic calibration with answer accuracy, yielding expected calibration error values between 0.30 and 0.50.
Injecting 100% numerical certainty into prompts results in lower accuracy compared to injecting 90% certainty.
Appending epistemic markers as prefixes before the answer results in significantly lower generation accuracy than placing them as suffixes after the answer.

limitations.text: Prior work on model epistemology primarily focused on linguistic calibration to ordinal outputs, ignoring naturalistic dimensions such as information sources, speaker commitment, and presupposition.
The evaluation filtered out multi-word and out-of-vocabulary answers to accurately measure token log probabilities, restricting analysis to single-word, high-frequency answers.
The study was restricted to English language trivia question answering and did not evaluate long-form text, multi-turn dialogue, or non-English cultural contexts.
Multi-shot prompting with epistemic markers was not comprehensively explored due to computational and time resource limitations.

future_work.text: Explore multi-shot prompting to significantly expand the exploration space of epistemic markers in language model contexts.
Investigate how models interpret expressions of uncertainty in long-form text generation and dialogue scenarios.
Examine syntactic, idiomatic, and pragmatic variations in epistemic markers across diverse non-English languages and cultural contexts.
Enable language models to accurately distinguish whether expressions of certainty are intended literally versus idiomatically.
Develop verified attribution mechanisms to prevent language models from generating unverified or false source attributions.

methodologies.name: Zero-Shot Epistemic Marker Prompt Injection
methodologies.description: Injecting 50 typology-categorized verbal and numerical expressions of certainty and uncertainty into open-ended trivia questions to evaluate model generation performance.
conditions: Tested across GPT-3 (davinci, Ada, Babbage, Curie), text-davinci-003, and GPT-4

methodologies.name: Pretraining Corpus Analysis of Uncertainty Markers
methodologies.description: Measuring occurrence frequencies and performing qualitative open coding on certainty and uncertainty expressions within question and answer posts in pretraining data.
conditions: Qualitative open coding on 100 sample instances
